notes: Both supplied units use the two-character string 趙倫 only as a historical exemplum of rebellion or usurpation, not as a biographical identification: 蕭勃干紀，非唯趙倫 and 為趙倫之事. Neither unit writes 司馬倫, 趙王, or any other alias. Treating 趙倫 as a shared full personal name would equate a possible surname-plus-given reading in Chen Shu with the conventional fief-plus-given label for Lun, Prince of Zhao, without an attested alias chain in these units. Compatible rebel dates and the inferred 司馬倫 claim are not independent proof. Keep the records separate as possible-same-as.
All three records share the full personal name 賈謐/Jia Mi; the Songshu aristocrat cut down before the Huainan disaster in Western Jin is compatible with the Jinshu courtier active AD 290–300.

Jinshu 053 explicitly identifies 南風 as the empress's name (南風，后名) for 賈后, who persecutes the crown prince and is later 賈庶人. Jinshu 032, in the empresses-consorts chapter, names 南風 as the woman who first treads the pepper palace (初踐椒宮) and whose cruelty topples the state (南風熾虐，國喪身傾). That is the same rare personal name 南風 for the Western Jin empress, attested as an alias of 賈后 and corroborated by the same palace-destruction narrative, not a title-only or chronology-only link. The supplied 032 units never write 賈南風; the merge rests on 南風 plus empress context.

Only these two supplied records write the full personal name 潘岳: 黃門侍郎潘岳 drafting the forged prayer, and 潘岳《金穀詩序》 as a literary benchmark. nanshi:043:p016 writes 安仁, not 潘岳; jinshu:117:p239 writes only 晉之潘、陸. Courtesy-name-only or surname-plus-Lu literary pairing is not a merge, and the proposal's statement that Nanshi shares 潘岳 is false on the Chinese. jinshu:117:p239 stays with its already-merged companion songshu:073:p067; that group is not pruned and is not pulled into this merge.

All four records share the full personal name 裴頠, with overlapping Western Jin activity around AD 267–300 and compatible official/scholar roles; English romanizations Pei Wei / Pei Yi / Pei Zhi are the same Chinese name.
